steps.say: This lesson shows how the kernel finds hardware and talks to it. A **driver** is the code for one kind of device. It also covers the most important rule here: the system only ever writes to a disk that is already its own.
Every driver is in kernel/drivers: disks (ahci, virtio_blk, nvme), network cards (e1000, r8169), sound (hda), input, the screen, and more.
**PCI** is the bus most devices sit on. At start the kernel lists every device once. Each driver then looks for the ones it knows, by their IDs or their class.

steps.anchor: /* The block layer: turns sector-granular disk drivers into /dev/sdX nodes
steps.through: * on, so user space can always start from /dev/sda. */
steps.say: The **block layer** sits between disk drivers and everything else. Drivers move whole sectors, fixed-size blocks of a disk. The block layer turns every disk into /dev/sda, /dev/sdb and so on, which can be read at any byte.

steps.anchor: /* Starting with the save slots' header (userland/shell/store.c), or, in a virtual machine only, blank in its first
steps.say: This is the rule. A disk is this system's only if it starts with the save header ("LUMENSTORE1", from the old working name). In a virtual machine, a blank new disk counts too.

steps.through: struct blkdev *p = blkdev_add_part(sda, first, sda->sectors - first, 2);
steps.say: `storage_init` starts the disk drivers, then makes every disk that isn't ours read-only. On ours, /dev/sda, the area from 320 MiB on becomes /dev/sda2, the data disk.

steps.say: It is enforced in one place that every write passes through. A read-only disk, or a part of one, answers EROFS, "read-only file system".
A disk that turns up later, like a USB stick, starts read-only and is checked the same way.

USB: xhci.c is the controller, hid.c handles keyboards, mice and tablets, msc.c handles sticks and drives. The commit that added them says they were written but not yet run, so treat them as untested.
`usb_init` registers the class drivers, then brings up every xHCI controller found on PCI. Each controller gets its own thread, so the start never waits for USB.

steps.anchor: /* NVMe (NVM Express): the SSDs of nearly every computer made since about 2016, all through one standard
steps.through: * disk (blkdev.c), one that isn't already this system's is read-only: a Windows SSD is never written. */
steps.say: NVMe is the standard for modern SSDs. Each NVMe disk follows the same rule. This driver is also marked written but not yet run.
The network: the Intel e1000 family and Realtek's r8169 chips (r8169 is new and not yet run either). DHCP asks the network for an address, and one network thread handles what arrives.
For a real PC with no serial port, "netlog" on the kernel command line sends the kernel's log over the local network. scripts/netlog.ps1 shows it on Windows. It is off unless asked for.

steps.anchor: /* The medium the system started from, read by the kernel (kernel/medium.h): optical drives as their drivers
steps.say: The CD the system started from is read by the kernel alone, in medium.c. It gets no /dev name, so the disks keep theirs.
